questions.problem: Find the limit  $\,{lim}_{t\to 2}f(t)$, if $f(t)={t}^{2}\,i+\frac{t-4}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{t}\,k.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, recall that:

$$
{lim}_{t\to 2}f(t)=({lim}_{t\to 2}{t}^{2})\,i+({lim}_{t\to 2}\frac{t-4}{2})\,j+({lim}_{t\to 2}\frac{1}{t})\,k
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- For the first component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}{t}^{2} & ={2}^{2}=4\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}\frac{t-4}{2} & =\frac{2-4}{2} \\  & =\frac{-2}{2} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}\frac{1}{t} & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{t\to 2}f(t)=4\,i-j+\frac{1}{2}\,k.$

questions.problem: Calculate ${lim}_{s\to 0}f(s)$, if $f(s)=⟨4{s}^{7}+13,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡s,\,\frac{{s}^{2}+13}{{e}^{s}}⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, recall that:

$$
{lim}_{s\to 0}f(s)=⟨{lim}_{s\to 0}(4{s}^{7}+13),\,{lim}_{s\to 0}2\operatorname{sin}⁡s,\,{lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{{s}^{2}+13}{{e}^{s}}⟩
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- For the first component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}(4{s}^{7}+13) & =4(0)^{7}+13=13\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}2\operatorname{sin}⁡s & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =2\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{{s}^{2}+13}{{e}^{s}} & =\frac{{0}^{2}+13}{{e}^{0}} \\  & =\frac{13}{1} \\  & =13\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{s\to 0}f(s)=⟨13,0,13⟩.$

First, recall that:

$$
{lim}_{s\to -2}f(s)=⟨{lim}_{s\to -2}(s+3)^{1/(s+2)},\,{lim}_{s\to -2}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(s+2)}{s+2},\,{lim}_{s\to -2}\frac{{s}^{2}+2s}{{s}^{2}+3s+2}⟩
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- The first component can be found using a special limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to -2}(s+3)^{1/(s+2)} & ={lim}_{s\to -2}(1+(s+2))^{1/(s+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{u\to 0}(1+u)^{1/u} \\  & =e\end{aligned}
$$

- The second component can be found using a special limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to -2}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(s+2)}{s+2} & ={lim}_{u\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡u}{u}=1\end{aligned}
$$

- The third component can be found using factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to -2}\frac{{s}^{2}+2s}{{s}^{2}+3s+2} & ={lim}_{s\to -2}\frac{s(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{s\to -2}\frac{s}{s+1} \\  & =\frac{-2}{-2+1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{s\to -2}f(s)=⟨e,1,2⟩.$

questions.problem: Calculate ${lim}_{t\to \pi }f(t),$ if $f(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\pi }{t} \\ \frac{2t}{\pi } \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi -t)}{\pi -t}\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, recall that

$$
{lim}_{t\to \pi }f(t)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\pi }{t} \\ {lim}_{t\to \pi }\frac{2t}{\pi } \\ {lim}_{t\to \pi }\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi -t)}{\pi -t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\pi }{t} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\pi }{\pi } \\  & =\frac{0-\pi }{\pi } \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }\frac{2t}{\pi } & =\frac{2\pi }{\pi }=2.\end{aligned}
$$

- The third component can be found using L'Hopital's Rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi -t)}{\pi -t} & ={lim}_{t\to \pi }\frac{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi -t))}^{′}}{(\pi -t)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{t\to \pi }\frac{-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi -t)}{(-1)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi -\pi )}{1} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{t\to \pi }f(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem: Find the limit  $\,{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t),$ if $f(t)=(1-{t}^{2})\,i+\frac{1}{t-1}\,j+\sqrt{1-t}\,k.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, recall that

$$
{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)=({lim}_{t\to 0}(1-{t}^{2}))i+({lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{t-1})j+({lim}_{t\to 0}\sqrt{t-1})k.
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}(1-{t}^{2}) & =1-{0}^{2}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{t-1}=\frac{1}{0-1}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\sqrt{1-t} & =\sqrt{1-0}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)=i-j+k.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Limit of the Magnitude of a Vector Function
questions.worked_solution:
First, recall that

$$
{lim}_{s\to 2}f(s)=⟨{lim}_{s\to 2}{e}^{s-2},\,{lim}_{s\to 2}\sqrt{6-s},\,{lim}_{s\to 2}\frac{3}{s+2}⟩.
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 2}{e}^{s-2} & ={e}^{2-2} \\  & ={e}^{0} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 2}\sqrt{6-s} & =\sqrt{6-2} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 2}\frac{3}{s+2} & =\frac{3}{2+2} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{s\to 2}f(s)=⟨1,2,\frac{3}{4}⟩.$

Finally, the limit of $‖f(s)‖$ as $s$ approaches $2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 2}‖f(s)‖ & =‖{lim}_{s\to 2}f(s)‖ \\  & =‖⟨1,2,\frac{3}{4}⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4+\frac{9}{16}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{89}{16}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{89}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}f(s) & =⟨{lim}_{s\to 0}{e}^{s},\,{lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{{s}^{2}-2}{s+6},\,{lim}_{s\to 0}{4}^{s}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- For the first component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}{e}^{s} & ={e}^{0}=1\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}\frac{{s}^{2}-2}{s+6} & =\frac{{0}^{2}-2}{0+6} \\  & =\frac{-2}{6} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}{4}^{s} & ={4}^{0}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{s\to 0}f(s)=⟨1,\,-\frac{1}{3},\,1⟩.$

Finally, the limit of $‖f(s)‖$ as $s$ approaches $0$ is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 0}‖f(s)‖ & =‖{lim}_{s\to 0}f(s)‖ \\  & =‖⟨1,\,-\frac{1}{3},\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{9}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{19}{9}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{19}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

First, recall that

$$
{lim}_{s\to 2}f(s)=⟨{lim}_{s\to 2}\frac{5}{{e}^{s-2}},\,{lim}_{s\to 2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4-2s),\,{lim}_{s\to 2}\,({s}^{3}-5)⟩.
$$

Now, we find the limits one by one.

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 2}\frac{5}{{e}^{s-2}} & =\frac{5}{{e}^{0}}=5.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4-2s) & =3{lim}_{s\to 2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4-2s) \\  & =3\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(4-2(0)) \\  & =3\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 2}\,({s}^{3}-5) & ={2}^{3}-5=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{s\to 2}f(s)=⟨5,3,3⟩.$

Finally, the limit of $‖f(s)‖$ as $s$ approaches $2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{s\to 2}‖f(s)‖ & =‖{lim}_{s\to 2}f(s)‖ \\  & =‖⟨5,3,3⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25+9+9} \\  & =\sqrt{43}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate ${lim}_{t\to 0}‖f(t)‖$, if $f(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡t}{t} \\ \frac{{e}^{-4t}-1}{t} \\ \frac{2{t}^{2}-8}{t-1}\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, recall that:

$$
{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡t}{t} \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{e}^{-4t}-1}{t} \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{2{t}^{2}-8}{t-1}\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- The first component can be found using a special limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡t}{t} & ={lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{t\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =({lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{t})\cdot ({lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}) \\  & =1\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡0}) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- The second can be found using L'Hopital's Rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{e}^{-4t}-1}{t} & ={lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{({e}^{-4t}-1)^{′}}{(t)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{-4{e}^{-4t}}{1} \\  & =-4{e}^{0} \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{2{t}^{2}-8}{t-1} & =\frac{2(0)^{2}-8}{(0)-1}=8\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4 \\ 8\end{aligned}].$

Finally, the limit of $‖f(t)‖$ as $t$ approaches $0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}‖f(t)‖ & =‖{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)‖ \\  & =‖[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4 \\ 8\end{aligned}]‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-4)^{2}+{8}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+16+64} \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find ${lim}_{t\to 1}[4f(t)-g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & ={t}^{2}\,i+t\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,k \\ g(t) & =\frac{3}{t}\,i+(4-t)\,j-({t}^{2}-1)\,k\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}f(t) & =({lim}_{t\to 1}{t}^{2})\,i+({lim}_{t\to 1}t)\,j+({lim}_{t\to 1}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\,k \\  & =({1}^{2})\,i+1\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡1\,k \\  & =1\,i+1\,j+0\,k \\  & =i+j, \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}g(t) & =({lim}_{t\to 1}\frac{3}{t})\,i+({lim}_{t\to 1}(4-t))\,j-({lim}_{t\to 1}({t}^{2}-1))\,k \\  & =\frac{3}{1}\,i+(4-1)\,j-({1}^{2}-1)\,k \\  & =3\,i+3\,j-0\,k \\  & =3\,i+3\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}[4f(t)-g(t)] & =4{lim}_{t\to 1}f(t)-{lim}_{t\to 1}g(t) \\  & =4(i+j)-(3\,i+3\,j) \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find ${lim}_{t\to 0}[2f(t)+3g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & ={t}^{2}\,i+(1+t)\,j-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\ g(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\,i-{e}^{t}\,j+(t-1)^{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t) & =({lim}_{t\to 0}{t}^{2})\,i+({lim}_{t\to 0}(1+t))\,j-({lim}_{t\to 0}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t))\,k \\  & =({0}^{2})\,i+(1+0)\,j-(\operatorname{sin}⁡0)\,k \\  & =0\,i+1\,j-0\,k \\  & =j, \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) & =({lim}_{t\to 0}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1))\,i-({lim}_{t\to 0}{e}^{t})\,j+({lim}_{t\to 0}(t-1)^{2})\,k \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡0-1)\,i-{e}^{0}\,j+(0-1)^{2}\,k \\  & =0\,i-1\,j+1\,k \\  & =-j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}[2f(t)+3g(t)] & =2{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)+3{lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) \\  & =2(j)+3(-j+k) \\  & =-j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \,-1}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \,-1}({t}^{2}+t) \\ {lim}_{t\to \,-1}{e}^{t+1} \\ {lim}_{t\to \,-1}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)}{t}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}(-1)^{2}+(-1) \\ {e}^{-1+1} \\ \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(-1+1)}{(-1)}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {lim}_{t\to \,-1}g(t)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \,-1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1) \\ {lim}_{t\to \,-1}2 \\ {lim}_{t\to \,-1}\frac{1-2t}{{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-1+1) \\ 2 \\ \frac{1-2(-1)}{(-1)^{2}+1})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \,-1}[3f(t)-2g(t)] & =3{lim}_{t\to \,-1}f(t)-2{lim}_{t\to \,-1}g(t) \\  & =3[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the limit ${lim}_{t\to 1}[f(t)\cdot g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨t,\,{t}^{2},\,{e}^{1-t}⟩ \\ g(t) & =⟨2t-{t}^{2},\,2t-1,\,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}f(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 1}\,t,\,{lim}_{t\to 1}\,{t}^{2},\,{lim}_{t\to 1}{e}^{1-t}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,{1}^{2},{e}^{1-1}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}g(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 1}\,(2t-{t}^{2}),\,{lim}_{t\to 1}\,(2t-1),\,{lim}_{t\to 1}3⟩ \\  & =⟨2(1)-{1}^{2},2(1)-1,3⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}[f(t)\cdot g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 1}f(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to 1}g(t) \\  & =⟨1,1,1⟩\cdot ⟨1,1,3⟩ \\  & =1(1)+1(1)+1(3) \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the limit ${lim}_{t\to 1}[f(t)\times g(t)]$ given that
$f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-1 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1)}{t-1}\end{aligned}],\,g(t)=[\begin{aligned}t+8 \\ \frac{4}{{t}^{2}+3} \\ 11\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}({t}^{2}-1) \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1)}{t-1}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{1}^{2}-1 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}g(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}(t+8) \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}\frac{4}{{t}^{2}+3} \\ {lim}_{t\to 1}11\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1+8 \\ \frac{4}{{1}^{2}+3} \\ 11\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 1 \\ 11\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we used the change of variable $u=t-1$ and the property ${lim}_{u\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡u}{u}=1.$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}[f(t)\times g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 1}f(t)\times {lim}_{t\to 1}g(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\times [\begin{aligned}9 \\ 1 \\ 11\end{aligned}] \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & \operatorname{sin}⁡1 & 1 \\ 9 & 1 & 11\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡1 & 1 \\ 1 & 11\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 9 & 11\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}0 & \operatorname{sin}⁡1 \\ 9 & 1\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡1\cdot 11-1\cdot 1)\,i-(0\cdot 11-1\cdot 9)\,j+(0\cdot 1-\operatorname{sin}⁡1\cdot 9)\,k \\  & =(11\operatorname{sin}⁡1-1)\,i+9\,j-9\operatorname{sin}⁡1k \\  & =[\begin{aligned}11\operatorname{sin}⁡1-1 \\ 9 \\ -9\operatorname{sin}⁡1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the limit ${lim}_{t\to \,-1}[f(t)\cdot g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+t \\ {e}^{t+1} \\ \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)}{t}\end{aligned}],\,g(t)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1) \\ 2 \\ \frac{1-2t}{{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \,-1}f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \,-1}({t}^{2}+t) \\ {lim}_{t\to \,-1}{e}^{t+1} \\ {lim}_{t\to \,-1}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)}{t}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}(-1)^{2}+(-1) \\ {e}^{-1+1} \\ \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(-1+1)}{(-1)}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {lim}_{t\to \,-1}g(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \,-1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1) \\ {lim}_{t\to \,-1}2 \\ {lim}_{t\to \,-1}\frac{1-2t}{{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-1+1) \\ 2 \\ \frac{1-2(-1)}{(-1)^{2}+1})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \,-1}[f(t)\cdot g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to \,-1}f(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to \,-1}g(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =0(0)+1(2)+(-1)(\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the limit ${lim}_{t\to 0}[f(t)\times g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{t}\,j+({t}^{2}+3)\,k \\ g(t) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)\,i+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{t}\,j+(t-2)^{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t) & =({lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+({lim}_{t\to 0}\sqrt{t})\,j+({lim}_{t\to 0}({t}^{2}+3))\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,i+\sqrt{0}\,j+({0}^{2}+3)\,k \\  & =1\,i+0\,j+3\,k \\  & =i+3\,k \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) & =({lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1))\,i+({lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{t})\,j+({lim}_{t\to 0}(t-2)^{2})\,k \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)\,i+1\,j+(0-2)^{2}\,k \\  & =0\,i+1\,j+4\,k \\  & =j+4\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the second component of ${lim}_{t\to \infty }g(t)$ is a special limit.

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}[f(t)\times g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 1}f(t)\times {lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) \\  & =(i+3\,k)\times (j+4\,k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(0\cdot 4-1\cdot 3)\,i-(1\cdot 4-0\cdot 3)\,j+(1\cdot 1-0\cdot 0)\,k \\  & =-3\,i-4\,j+1\,k \\  & =-3i-4\,j+k\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the limit ${lim}_{t\to \infty }[f(t)\cdot g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨{e}^{-t},\,{(1+\frac{1}{t})}^{t},\,4⟩ \\ g(t) & =⟨\frac{{t}^{2}}{1-{t}^{2}},\,\frac{t+1}{t},\,{t}^{-5}⟩\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }f(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to \infty }{e}^{-t},\,{lim}_{t\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{t})}^{t},\,{lim}_{t\to \infty }4⟩ \\  & =⟨0,e,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the second component of ${lim}_{t\to \infty }f(t)$ is a special limit.

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }g(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{{t}^{2}}{1-{t}^{2}},\,{lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{t+1}{t},\,{lim}_{t\to \infty }{t}^{-5}⟩ \\  & =⟨{lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}-1)},\,1+{lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{1}{t},\,{lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{1}{{t}^{5}}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }[f(t)\cdot g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to \infty }f(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to \infty }g(t) \\  & =⟨0,\,e,\,4⟩\cdot ⟨-1,1,0⟩ \\  & =0\cdot (-1)+e\cdot 1+4\cdot 0 \\  & =e\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Calculate  $\lim\limits_{t \to 0} \mathbf{f}(t),$ given that 

$$
\mathbf f (t) = \dfrac{1- e^{t}}{\sin t} \ \mathbf {i}+ \dfrac{\sin t}{t+t^2} \ \mathbf {j} + \dfrac{ e^{t} - e^{-t}}{\sin t} \ \mathbf {k}.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the limit of our vector function, we compute the limit of each component individually:

$$
\lim_{t \to 0}\mathbf f(t) = \left(\lim_{t \to 0} \dfrac{1-e^t}{\sin t}\right)\,\mathbf i + \left( \lim_{t \to 0} \dfrac{\sin t}{t+t^2}\right)\,\mathbf j + \left( \lim_{t \to 0} \dfrac{e^t-e^{-t}}{\sin t} \right)\,\mathbf k
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- The first component can be found using L'Hopital's Rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{1-{e}^{t}}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} & ={lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{(1-{e}^{t})}^{′}}{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{-{e}^{t}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{-{e}^{0}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡0} \\  & =-\frac{1}{1} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

- The second component can be found using a special limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{t+{t}^{2}} & ={lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{t(t+1)} \\  & =({lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{t+1})\cdot ({lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{t}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{0+1})\cdot 1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- The third component can be found using L'Hopital's Rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{e}^{t}-{e}^{-t}}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} & ={lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{({e}^{t}-{e}^{-t})}^{′}}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{e}^{t}+{e}^{-t}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{0}+{e}^{-0}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡0} \\  & =\frac{1+1}{1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\lim\limits_{t \to 0}\mathbf f(t) = -\mathbf i + \mathbf j +2\,\mathbf k.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Limit of the Magnitude of a Vector Function
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the limit of our vector function, we compute the limit of each component individually:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }f(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to \infty }{t}^{-1},\,{lim}_{t\to \infty }{(1+\frac{3}{t})}^{t},\,{lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{{t}^{2}}{1-{t}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }{t}^{-1} & ={lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{1}{t}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

- The second component can be found using a special limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }{(1+\frac{3}{t})}^{t} & ={lim}_{t\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{t/3})}^{t/3}]}^{3} \\  & ={[{lim}_{t\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{t/3})}^{t/3}]}^{3} \\  & =[\,e\,]^{3} \\  & ={e}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{{t}^{2}}{1-{t}^{2}} & ={lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{1}{\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}-1}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\lim\limits_{t \to \infty}\mathbf f(t) = \left\langle 0, \: e^3, \: -1\right\rangle.
$$

Finally, the limit of $\left\| \mathbf f(t) \right\|$ as $t$ approaches $\infty$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }‖f(t)‖ & =‖{lim}_{t\to \infty }f(t)‖ \\  & =‖⟨0,\,{e}^{3},\,-1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+({e}^{3})^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{e}^{6}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find $\displaystyle \lim_{t \to 0} \big[ \mathbf f(t) - 2 \mathbf g(t) \big]$ given that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{t} \\ t\end{aligned}],\,g(t)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 1 \\ 2t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}{e}^{t} \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\ {e}^{0} \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}g(t)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}1 \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}2t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\ 1 \\ 2(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}[f(t)-2g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)-2{lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find $\displaystyle \lim_{t \to 2} \left[\mathbf f(t) \cdot \mathbf g(t)\right]$ given that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are defined as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+t\,j+{t}^{2}\,k \\ g(t) & =(2-t)\,i+\frac{6}{t}\,j-4\,k\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}f(t) & =({lim}_{t\to 2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\,i+({lim}_{t\to 2}t)\,j+({lim}_{t\to 2}{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\,i+2\,j+{2}^{2}\,k \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,i+2\,j+4\,k, \\ {lim}_{t\to 2}g(t) & =({lim}_{t\to 2}(2-t))\,i+({lim}_{t\to 2}\frac{6}{t})\,j+({lim}_{t\to 2}(-4))\,k \\  & =(2-2)\,i+\frac{6}{2}\,j+(-4)\,k \\  & =0\,i+3\,j-4\,k \\  & =3\,j-4\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}[f(t)\cdot g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 2}f(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to 2}g(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,i+2\,j+4\,k)\cdot (3\,j-4\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot 0+2\cdot 3+4\cdot (-4) \\  & =-10\end{aligned}
$$
